title: Midterm Election Flips: What They Really Mean For Your Retirement Savings
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Congress just flipped. Wall Street says "cash is trash." But the quietest wealthy retirees were already holding cash before election night, and history shows why.

In this video, we walk through the four midterm waves that flipped Washington (1946, 1994, 2010 and 2026), what the stock market actually did after each one, and why the two "close calls" hurt retirees months after the vote, not on election night. Then we break down the difference between fear cash and plan cash, what a divided Congress really means for your Social Security, Medicare and taxes, and four simple steps to build your own "storm shelter" before the next siren.

This is not a political video. We don't judge any result. We only follow the money.

CHAPTERS 0:00 The knock on the door 2:10 Four sirens since 1946 5:47 1946, 1994, 2010 and the week of 2026 14:14 Fear cash vs. plan cash (and what a divided Congress changes) 20:58 4 steps to build your shelter 24:48 Why "cash is trash" is the wrong advice for retirees 27:30 What Otis wrote in 1994

SOURCES Election results and history

title: What Percentage Of Retirees Still Carry A Mortgage?

description:

title: The Insurance Cost That Quietly Separates Comfortable Retirees From Struggling Ones

description:

The cheapest is about $9,800 a year and the most expensive tops $16,000. We compare Medigap and Medicare Advantage, look at a lean stack against the full stack people carry from their working years, and show which bill wins in a healthy year and in a bad one.

title: Where Quiet Wealth Retirees Actually Live?

description:
Most retirees with quiet wealth never move to Florida. They stay right where they are, and the data shows why. In this video, we walk through a simple 5-step “address test” to see whether the place you already live is a quiet-wealth address, and what leaving it would really cost before you list the house.

description:

title: How Much Do Retirees Really Pay In Property Taxes?
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
What does a retiree actually pay in property taxes — the number on the chart, or the number after senior relief? We follow a hypothetical couple, both 67, comparing the same $320,000 house in New Jersey, Texas and Colorado. On paper, New Jersey is the most expensive state in America. After New Jersey's Stay NJ credit, Texas's over-65 exemption and school tax freeze, and Colorado's senior exemption, the real ranking looks very different — and the 20-year totals may surprise you.

In this video:
What households 65+ really pay in property taxes (BLS data)
Exemptions, freezes and credits — how senior relief works
New Jersey's Stay NJ program (and how it changed in 2026)

title: What Type of Retiree Are You 5 Clear Signs
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Researchers surveyed nearly 6,000 Americans who were retired or close to it — and found that people in the heart of retirement fall into four distinct paths. In this video, we walk through all four, and the 5 clear signs that show which one you're on (or heading toward, if you haven't retired yet).

Money matters, but it's only one of the five signs. Purpose, health and the people around you make up the rest — and the data shows your path isn't fixed. More than half of retirees make changes along the way.

Are you in the top 10% of retirees? By net worth alone, that bar starts around $3 million — and most people never get near it. But money is only one way to measure a retirement.
